title: Dependency provenance, lockfiles, and safe upgrades
sources: Python Packaging User Guide: dependency specification and distribution concepts
pip documentation: Secure installs — Hash-checking Mode (reviewed 2026-10-03)
masterChecklist: Secure dependency lifecycle: provenance, pinning, advisories, SBOM concepts, license review, upgrade strategy
Virtual environments, interpreter selection, pip boundaries and dependency isolation
Version upgrades and compatibility testing; language-feature gates and feature detection
whyItMatters: Every package extends a Python application's code and risk surface. Reproducible dependencies make failures diagnosable; careful upgrades reduce surprise breakage and let teams respond deliberately to security advisories.
simpleExplanation: A dependency declaration describes what a project can use. A resolved/locked set records the exact versions selected for a tested environment. Provenance asks where a package came from and whether it is the intended artifact. A safe upgrade reviews impact, tests representative behavior, records the change, and keeps a rollback option.
mentalModel: Dependencies are ingredients in a restaurant kitchen. The menu may say ‘flour’, but a reliable kitchen records the supplier and batch it actually used so a problem can be traced and corrected.
outcomes: Distinguish a broad dependency requirement from a tested resolved version set.
Use isolated environments for project dependencies.
Recognize advisory, provenance, license, and transitive-dependency review needs.
Plan an upgrade as a tested change rather than an automatic version bump.
Avoid installing unreviewed packages or secrets-bearing install commands blindly.

realWorldExample.scenario: A project needs to update a package after a security advisory.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: The team upgrades every package at once in a shared environment, cannot tell what changed, and has no test/rollback evidence when an import or production workflow breaks.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Identify the affected direct/transitive package, review supported fixed versions and compatibility notes, update in an isolated environment, run tests and representative flows, record the resolved set/change reason, and plan rollback or follow-up migration.

workedExample.code:
upgrade_plan = {
    'package': 'example-library',
    'reason': 'security advisory review',
    'from_version': '1.2.0',
    'to_version': '1.2.3',
    'checks': ['unit tests', 'progress-import sample', 'deployment smoke check'],
    'rollback': 'restore the previous tested resolved set if compatibility fails'
}
print(upgrade_plan['checks'])
explanation: This is a planning record, not a command to install a package.
The exact project tooling may use a requirements/lock mechanism or another resolver, but the release questions remain the same.
The plan records why the change happened, what was tested, and what to do if it fails.
Transitive dependencies also matter because a direct package can introduce or update them.
Never copy package installation instructions from an untrusted source into a privileged environment without review.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add an affected API/import to the checks. Explain why a green unit suite alone may not prove deployment compatibility.

procedure: Use an isolated environment and record the interpreter/tooling context.
Identify direct and transitive dependencies relevant to the change.
Review package source/provenance, advisory/fix information, license/policy requirements, and compatibility notes through approved channels.
Update the smallest justified set first and capture the tested resolved versions.
Run automated tests plus representative import/build/deployment checks.
Record release notes, known migration needs, and rollback path.
Schedule follow-up review for deprecated or vulnerable dependencies rather than silently ignoring them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Installing packages globally for every project.
commonMistakes.why: Projects can interfere with each other's versions and reproduce poorly.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use a project-specific environment and record dependencies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Updating all dependencies only because one needs a fix.
commonMistakes.why: It increases change surface and makes failures harder to attribute.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a lockfile as a security guarantee.
commonMistakes.why: It improves reproducibility but does not by itself verify package trust, vulnerabilities, or behavior.
commonMistakes.avoid: Combine version records with review, advisories, tests, and policy.

lab.solutionExplanation: The plan makes an upgrade reviewable and reproducible. It does not install anything because safe installation needs the project’s approved environment, resolver, sources, and verification process.

projectConnection.milestone: Create a dependency inventory and one upgrade plan with source/advisory review, tested resolved versions, representative checks, release note, and rollback decision.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The project can explain what changed and why, reproduce the tested dependency set, demonstrate relevant checks, and avoid claiming that a lockfile alone proves security.

assessment.question: What does a resolved/locked dependency set help with?
assessment.answer: It records the exact dependency versions tested together so environments are more reproducible.
assessment.explanation: It does not replace security and compatibility review.

assessment.question: Why isolate environments per project?
assessment.answer: Different projects can need different versions without interfering with each other.
assessment.explanation: Isolation improves repeatability and reduces accidental coupling.

assessment.question: Why include a rollback plan for upgrades?
assessment.answer: A compatibility problem may appear only in a representative flow or deployment, and recovery needs to be deliberate.
assessment.explanation: Rollback is part of release safety.
